title: Loving Jesus above all (II.7)
hookLine: love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself
tomorrow: can you be close friends with someone you can't see?

cards: Second place sounds like losing. So a phrase like love Jesus above all can land badly with the people we love most: a best friend, a partner, a kid. Wait, so I'm fourth?

Some readers wrestle with chapter seven of book two of the Imitation for exactly that reason. It's short, it's intense, and the whole thing turns on one sentence: love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself.
Two readings of it pull in different directions. Both deserve a hearing.

teach.h: CLING, AND YOU FALL WITH IT.
teach.b: Here's the case that the chapter is hard on human love. It says the love of creatures is deceitful and unstable, and whoever clings to a creature falls with the falling thing.
Don't lean on a reed shaken by the wind, it warns, because all flesh is grass, a phrase it borrows from Isaiah.
Some readers hear a monk's caution in that, written for men who had left home, and say ordinary life needs warmer words for a mother, a spouse, a friend.
On that view, the chapter is true for the cloister and needs translating for the kitchen table. Now the case that the chapter is generous.
Its key line doesn't say love Jesus instead of everyone. It says love all for Jesus, in Latin, propter Iesum, for his sake. On that reading nobody is demoted.

Everyone else is loved through him, and he's loved for no reason beyond himself, so love for a friend doesn't fall when things fall. The chapter even promises a friend who won't leave when everyone else goes away.
Catholic teaching holds the two commandments together: love God with your whole heart, and your neighbor as yourself.
So both readings agree the friend matters, and both agree on the order. What they argue about is tone: whether the order should sound like a warning, or like a wider embrace.

how: Catholics speak of loving God above all as the first commandment, joined to love of neighbor, and some readers of the Imitation pray for the people they love by name, offering them to Christ.

the line is love all for Jesus: everyone else loved for his sake, not less.

games.q: your friend says the Imitation's warning about clinging to creatures sounds cold toward her family. what's the best case for her side?
o: it was written for monks who'd left home; family life may need warmer words.
she just doesn't like old books very much.
people should always come first, whatever anyone believes.
games.why: that's her view at its strongest, and some Catholic readers share it. the other reading points to 'love all for Jesus': nobody demoted.

practice: Count on your fingers the people you love, one by one, until you reach five or run out of fingers. Give each one a second of thanks as the finger goes down. If you pray, hold each one up to Jesus, for his sake.
Either way, notice that you can love each one without gripping.

wordCard.voice: Loving Jesus above all. The Imitation's order of love: love everyone and everything for Jesus' sake, and Jesus for himself.

orig.note: Latin, from the Imitation II.7: for Jesus' sake. love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: above all, not instead of everyone else, but holding them all up. Until tomorrow.
